l: Hebron, 1 Chronicles
s: Hebron is the place where David reigned seven years and six months and where six sons were born to him. Israel's elders came there to covenant with him and anoint him king, and the tribes' armed men gathered, wholehearted, to transfer Saul's kingdom to David, feasting three days.

l: Jerusalem, 1 Chronicles
s: Jerusalem, also called Jebus, is a city that serves as a dwelling place and royal seat. Records show Benjamite family heads, including lines of Shaharaim, Mikloth, and Jeiel's relatives, living there. Later, people of Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh, along with priests, Levites, and gatekeepers, are listed as residents. David reigned there thirty-three years, and nine sons were born to him, including Solomon. After his anointing, David and all Israel go there, take the Jebusite stronghold of Zion, and make it David's city, built around from Millo, with Joab repairing the rest.

l: Solomon, 1 Chronicles
s: Solomon is a son of David, born in Jerusalem to Bathshua daughter of Ammiel, and the father of Rehoboam, who begins the line of succeeding kings. The records first present him through the LORD's promise to David: a son who will follow him, build the LORD a house, have his throne established forever, be treated as a son by the LORD, and never lose the LORD's loving kindness as David's predecessor did. David then names Solomon as that son. He is described as young and tender, yet alone chosen by the LORD out of many to sit on the throne of the LORD's kingdom over Israel and to build the temple and its courts. His name is tied to peace, as a man of peace who receives rest from his enemies. David charges him to keep the law, be strong and courageous, serve God with a perfect heart and willing mind, and warns he will be cast off if he forsakes God. David gives him the temple plans and tells him skilled, willing workers will assist in all kinds of work. Solomon is made king over Israel by the aged David, and is made king a second time and anointed before the LORD. He sits on the LORD's throne and prospers. All Israel, the princes, the mighty men, and David's other sons submit to him, and the LORD magnifies him with royal majesty greater than any previous king of Israel. He also makes the bronze sea, pillars and vessels from bronze of Tibhath and Cun.

l: Rehoboam, 1 Chronicles
s: has_son Abijah Rehoboam is named as Solomon's son. He heads the list of royal descendants, followed by Abijah his son, then Asa and Jehoshaphat.

l: Manasseh, 1 Chronicles
s: Manasseh is a patriarchal figure whose concubine, the Aramitess, bore his son Asriel and Machir, father of Gilead. The records trace his descendants through Machir and Gilead, and note that his children's borders adjoin settlements: Beth Shean, Taanach, Megiddo and Dor.

l: Josiah, 1 Chronicles
s: Josiah, son of Amon, ends the royal succession in Chapter 3 and fathers four sons: Johanan, Jehoiakim, Zedekiah, and Shallum.

l: Jeconiah, 1 Chronicles
s: Jeconiah, son of Jehoiakim and called the captive, is listed as father of seven sons, including Shealtiel and Pedaiah.

l: Zerubbabel, 1 Chronicles
s: Zerubbabel, a person, son of Pedaiah alongside Shimei, fathered Meshullam, Hananiah and daughter Shelomith, plus five more children listed afterward.

l: God, 1 Chronicles
s: God, called the God of Israel, is portrayed as a deity who hears and answers those who cry out and trust him. He grants Jabez's requests for blessing, an enlarged border, and protection. He helps Reuben, Gad, and half-Manasseh against the Hagrites, yet after their trespass stirs up Pul and Tilgath Pilneser to carry them into exile. He guides David in battle against the Philistines, first promising deliverance, then directing a flanking approach by the mulberry trees, and David credits him with breaking his enemies. Finally, he forbids David to build the house because of shed blood, promising Solomon, who will build it, and peace and rest for Israel.

l: Benaiah, 1 Chronicles
s: Benaiah, son of Jehoiada of Kabzeel, is a valiant warrior and priest's son. He killed the two sons of Ariel of Moab, a lion in a pit on a snowy day, and a five-cubit Egyptian with the Egyptian's own spear. Renowned among the thirty yet not attaining to the three, he was set by David over his guard, leading the Cherethites and Pelethites, and commanded the third monthly division of twelve.

l: Simeonite princes, 1 Chronicles
s: Simeonite princes, heads of families whose fathers' houses increased greatly, sought pasture at Gedor's entrance, found it rich and peaceful, and in Hezekiah's days destroyed the Meunim there and settled in their place.

l: Simeonite expedition to Mount Seir, 1 Chronicles
s: Five hundred Simeonite men, led by Ishi's sons Pelatiah, Neariah, Rephaiah and Uzziel, went to Mount Seir, struck the Amalekite remnant who had escaped, and settled there, living in the land to this day.

l: Reubenites, 1 Chronicles
s: The Reubenites descend from Reuben's sons Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi, with Beerah as prince. Their livestock spread them from Aroer to Nebo, Baal Meon, and eastward in Gilead. They fought the Hagrites alongside allies and were later carried away by Assyria.

l: Beerah, 1 Chronicles
s: Beerah, son of Baal in Joel's line, was a Reubenite prince whom Tilgath Pilneser, king of Assyria, carried away captive.

l: Tilgath Pilneser, 1 Chronicles
s: is_a king of Assyria Tilgath Pilneser, king of Assyria, carried Beerah the Reubenite prince away captive. God stirred up his spirit, and he carried the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh to Halah, Habor, Hara, and the river of Gozan.

l: Saul, 1 Chronicles
s: Saul, son of Kish and descended through Ner, fathered Jonathan, Malchishua, Abinadab, and Eshbaal. He is remembered for his trespass against the LORD, notably consulting one with a familiar spirit instead of the LORD. David fled from him, though Benjamin's kinsmen largely kept allegiance to his house until they backed David. In battle at Mount Gilboa, archers overtook him; when his armor bearer refused to kill him, he fell on his own sword. The Philistines stripped his body and displayed his head and armor in their gods' houses, while the men of Jabesh Gilead buried him, and his kingdom turned to David.

l: Hagrites, 1 Chronicles
s: is_defeated_in war against the Hagrites [delivered into the hands of Reubenites, Gadites, Manasseh] The Hagrites were fought in the days of Saul and fell by the hand of the Reubenites, who lived in their tents east of Gilead. In a later war, with Jetur, Naphish, and Nodab, they were delivered into the hands of Reuben, Gad, and half-Manasseh, who took their camels, sheep, donkeys, and men.

l: Gadites, 1 Chronicles
s: The Gadites are a tribe who lived beside the Reubenites in Bashan as far as Salecah, with chiefs including Joel, Shapham, Janai, and Shaphat, recorded by genealogy in the days of Jotham and Jeroboam. They fought the Hagrites alongside Reuben and half of Manasseh, who were delivered into their hand, but were later carried into exile by Assyrian kings. Some Gadites joined David as mighty men of valor, lion-faced and gazelle-swift, serving as army captains and crossing the Jordan to rout valley dwellers.

l: Manasseh, 1 Chronicles
s: Manasseh is a half-tribe that settled and multiplied from Bashan to Baal Hermon, Senir, and Mount Hermon, led by mighty heads of fathers' houses. Early on it joined war against the Hagrites, but then committed idolatry, following the gods of the land's peoples. Elsewhere, captains of thousands such as Adnah and Zillethai aided David at Ziklag, and eighteen thousand came to Hebron to make him king. Because of its trespass, the tribe was carried off to Assyrian captivity at Halah, Habor, Hara, and Gozan.

l: Pul, 1 Chronicles
s: is_a king of Assyria Pul is a king of Assyria whose spirit the God of Israel stirred up. He is named together with Tilgath Pilneser in the carrying away of the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh.

l: war against the Hagrites, 1 Chronicles
s: is_a war of God Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, with 44,760 valiant men able to go to war, fought the Hagrites, Jetur, Naphish, and Nodab. They were helped because they cried to God and trusted him, and the enemy fell into their hands. They took 50,000 camels, 250,000 sheep, 2,000 donkeys, and 100,000 men, and lived in their place until the captivity.

l: Assyrian captivity, 1 Chronicles
s: is_carried_out_by Tilgath Pilneser God stirred up Pul and Tilgath Pilneser, kings of Assyria, who carried the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh away. They were brought to Halah, Habor, Hara, and the river of Gozan, where they remain to this day.

l: idolatry (trespass of Manasseh half-tribe), 1 Chronicles
s: The heads of the half-tribe of Manasseh trespassed against the God of their fathers and played the prostitute after the gods of the peoples of the land whom God had destroyed before them. This unfaithfulness precedes God's stirring up of the Assyrian kings to carry them into exile.

l: Gershom, 1 Chronicles
s: Gershom is a son of Levi, father of Libni and Shimei, with a line through Libni to Jeatherai and ancestor of Asaph; his sons received thirteen cities from Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Manasseh.

l: Kohath, 1 Chronicles
s: Kohath, a son of Levi, fathered Amram, Izhar, Hebron and Uzziel. Aaron's priestly line and Heman the singer descend from him. His families received cities by lot: thirteen for Aaron's sons, ten for the rest.

l: Merari, 1 Chronicles
s: Merari, a son of Levi, fathered Mahli and Mushi; Ethan, a left-hand singer, descends from him; his sons received twelve cities by lot from Reuben, Gad, and Zebulun.

l: Aaron, 1 Chronicles
s: Aaron is a son of Amram, brother of Moses and Miriam, of the Kohathites, and father of Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. He and his sons were separated forever to sanctify the most holy things: burning incense, ministering, and blessing in the LORD's name. They offered on the altars and made atonement for Israel as Moses commanded. Later, the ordering of priestly service follows the ordinance he gave, as the LORD commanded him.

l: Eleazar, 1 Chronicles
s: Eleazar, a priest who survived childless Nadab and Abihu, headed a line with sixteen chief fathers' houses, outnumbering Ithamar's, and Zadok descended from him.

l: Ithamar, 1 Chronicles
s: Ithamar served as priest alongside Eleazar after Nadab and Abihu died childless; his line had eight fathers' houses heads and includes Ahimelech.

l: Zadok, 1 Chronicles
s: Zadok is a priest, son of Ahitub, descended from Eleazar. Early he is a young mighty man of valor with twenty-two captains. He serves before the LORD's tabernacle at Gibeon, offering daily burnt offerings, helps David divide the priestly orders, and is anointed at Solomon's accession.

l: Asaph, 1 Chronicles
s: Asaph, son of Berechiah and brother of Heman, is a Levite singer whose lineage traces back to Levi through Gershom. He stood at Heman's right hand in the service of song. David made him chief of the appointed Levites, who sound cymbals and minister continually before God's ark. He prophesied at the king's order, and his four sons served under him; the first lot fell to Joseph.

l: Hashabiah, 1 Chronicles
s: Hashabiah, a Hebronite, with his brothers, 1,700 men of valor, oversaw Israel west of the Jordan for all the LORD's business and the king's service.

l: Levites, 1 Chronicles
s: The Levites are the descendants of Levi through Gershon (Gershom), Kohath, and Merari, chosen by the LORD to carry God's ark and minister forever. Those not priests were appointed to all the service of the tabernacle of God's house, and the children of Israel gave them cities with pasture lands by lot. Records list members such as Shemaiah, Mattithiah, and others who served as gatekeepers, keepers of vessels and baked goods, and singers living in the rooms, free from other service and working day and night. When the ark was moved, only Levites were to carry it; family heads gathered, sanctified themselves, and bore it on their shoulders with poles as Moses commanded, with sacrifices of seven bulls and seven rams. David then appointed some to minister before the ark with harps, stringed instruments, and cymbals, and others as doorkeepers and givers of thanks. Those aged thirty and up numbered thirty-eight thousand, divided under the three sons of Levi. Because the LORD dwells in Jerusalem, they no longer carry the tabernacle; instead they wait on the sons of Aaron, oversee the LORD's house, and offer morning and evening thanks. Finally, the remaining Levites cast lots before David, as the sons of Aaron did, with Shemaiah son of Nethanel as scribe.

l: sons of Aaron, 1 Chronicles
s: The sons of Aaron are Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar, a priestly family. Nadab and Abihu died childless before their father, so only Eleazar and Ithamar served as priests. Eleazar's line continues through Phinehas and Zadok down to Jehozadak. They were set apart forever for the most holy things, incense, ministry, and blessing, with Levites serving them. They received thirteen cities, including Hebron and Libnah, with Hebron the Kohathites' first lot.

l: Judah, 1 Chronicles
s: Judah is a tribal group whose men joined David at Hebron, 6,800 armed with shield and spear, with some pledging loyalty earlier; it was later carried captive to Babylon for disobedience.

l: Benjamin, 1 Chronicles
s: Benjamin is a tribe, Saul's own, with sons Bela, Becher, and Jediael, whose lines were counted as mighty warriors (Bela's 22,034). Later it supplied David with ambidextrous archers and slingers; at Hebron three thousand came, though most had kept allegiance to Saul's house until then.

l: Levite cities with pasture lands, 1 Chronicles
s: is_given_by Israel [children of Israel gave to the Levites] The cities with pasture lands were given to the Levites by lot from across the tribes. Thirteen went to Aaron's sons, ten to the rest of the Kohathites, thirteen to the Gershomites, and twelve to the Merarites. The fields and villages of Hebron went to Caleb the son of Jephunneh.

l: service of song (David's appointed singers), 1 Chronicles
s: David set the singers over the service of song after the ark came to rest. Heman the Kohathite, Asaph the Gershomite, and Ethan the Merarite served in order, with Asaph on Heman's right and the Merarites on the left. They ministered before the tabernacle until Solomon built the LORD's house in Jerusalem.

l: LORD's house, 1 Chronicles
s: The LORD's house is a planned temple to be built for the name of the LORD God, meant to be exceedingly magnificent and famous throughout all countries. It will house the ark of the covenant and the holy vessels. David declares its site and appoints Solomon to build it. Twenty-four thousand Levites oversee the work and serve in its courts, rooms, and offerings, while doorkeepers guard its gates and storehouse, treasurers manage its treasures, and battle plunder is dedicated to its repair.

l: God's ark, 1 Chronicles
s: The ark is God the LORD's ark, belonging to the LORD and sitting above the cherubim. Moved on a new cart from Abinadab's house toward David's city, it stopped when Uzza touched it and the LORD struck him dead. It was diverted to Obed-Edom's house for three months. The Levites then carried it on their shoulders with poles, as Moses commanded, amid sacrifices, music and shouting, and set it in the middle of David's tent, where offerings were made and Asaph and his brothers ministered continually.

l: Tola, 1 Chronicles
s: Tola is a father of six sons (Uzzi, Rephaiah, Jeriel, Jahmai, Ibsam, Shemuel), each head of a father's house and mighty men of valor; their descendants numbered 22,600 fighting men in David's days.

l: Ephraim, 1 Chronicles
s: Ephraim is a patriarch whose sons include Shuthelah, Ezer, Elead, and later Beriah. Ezer and Elead were killed by the men of Gath over livestock, and Ephraim mourned while his brothers comforted him. Beriah was born afterward. His line continues to Nun and Joshua, and his children settled Bethel, Gezer, Shechem, and other places.

l: Beriah (son of Ephraim), 1 Chronicles
s: Beriah, son of Ephraim, was born after his brothers' deaths and named for trouble in his father's house; he fathered Sheerah and Rephah.

l: Sheerah, 1 Chronicles
s: Sheerah, a daughter of Ephraim's house in Beriah's line, is recorded as builder of lower and upper Beth Horon and Uzzen Sheerah.

l: Uzza, 1 Chronicles
s: drives cart [with Ahio] Uzza, with Ahio, drove the cart carrying the ark. At Chidon's threshing floor he put out his hand to hold the ark when the oxen stumbled, and the LORD's anger burned against him so that he died there before God. The place was called Perez Uzza.

l: Shaharaim, 1 Chronicles
s: Shaharaim is a man with three wives, Hushim, Baara and Hodesh. After sending children away he fathered others in Moab's field. By Hodesh he had seven children, led by Jobab, head of a fathers' household; by Hushim he had Abitub and Elpaal.

l: priests, 1 Chronicles
s: The priests are a group serving God's house. Named members include Jedaiah, Jehoiarib, Jachin, and Azariah, its ruler, with 1,760 able kinsmen, heads of fathers' houses. Descended from Eleazar and Ithamar, they were divided by lot into twenty-four orders, sixteen and eight, each serving its appointed time per Aaron's ordinance.

l: Jeduthun, 1 Chronicles
s: Jeduthun is a man who prophesied with the harp, giving thanks and praising the LORD under the king's order; his six sons, named Gedaliah through Mattithiah, served under his hands, including as gatekeepers.

l: gatekeepers, 1 Chronicles
s: The gatekeepers are a group of 212 men chosen to guard the gates of God's house, led by chief Shallum with Akkub, Talmon, and Ahiman. Ordained by David and Samuel in an office of trust, they were stationed on four sides, relieved every seven days by brothers from villages, opened the house each morning, and four chief Levites oversaw the rooms and treasuries.

l: Meshelemiah, 1 Chronicles
s: Meshelemiah, a Korahite doorkeeper son of Kore, had seven sons, Zechariah the firstborn through Eliehoenai the seventh. Together with his sons and brothers he counted eighteen valiant men among the doorkeepers.

l: God's house, 1 Chronicles
s: God's house is the temple intended as a dwelling for the LORD's name and a house of rest for the ark of the covenant and God's footstool. David wished to replace the ark's tent with a house, but the LORD forbade him and said his offspring would build it. David then gave Solomon detailed plans covering the porch, rooms, treasuries, courts, mercy seat place, and vessels, and prepared gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood, and stones. It is to be served by organized divisions of priests and Levites and skilled willing workers. Gatekeepers guard its four sides, oversee its rooms and treasuries, and caretakers manage vessels, furniture, and provisions. David prays Solomon will have a perfect heart to build it.

l: singers, 1 Chronicles
s: is_a heads of fathers' households of the Levites [lived in the rooms, free from other service, employed day and night] David directed the Levite chiefs to appoint singers with stringed instruments, harps, and cymbals to sound aloud with joy. Heman, Asaph, and Ethan were given bronze cymbals, others played stringed instruments set to Alamoth and harps tuned to the eight-stringed lyre, and Chenaniah, chief of the Levites, taught them because he was skillful. They wore fine linen robes in the procession.

l: Mount Gilboa, 1 Chronicles
s: Mount Gilboa is where the men of Israel fall slain and where Saul and his sons die. The Philistines find the fallen bodies of Saul and his sons there the next day.

l: sons of Saul, 1 Chronicles
s: Three sons of Saul, Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua, are killed by the Philistines, who pursue hard after them. They die together with Saul, and their bodies are later taken by the valiant men of Jabesh Gilead and their bones buried under the oak in Jabesh.

l: Jabesh Gilead, 1 Chronicles
s: All Jabesh Gilead hears what the Philistines did to Saul. In response its valiant men take the bodies of Saul and his sons, bring them to Jabesh, and bury their bones under the oak there; the people fast seven days.

l: valiant men of Jabesh Gilead, 1 Chronicles
s: Valiant men from Jabesh Gilead retrieve the bodies of Saul and his sons, bring them to Jabesh, bury the bones under the oak, and fast seven days.

l: Battle at Mount Gilboa, 1 Chronicles
s: took_place_at Mount Gilboa The battle goes against Israel as the Philistines put its men to flight and many fall slain on Mount Gilboa. Saul's three sons are killed, Saul is distressed by the archers, and the Israelites in the valley afterward abandon their cities.

l: Saul's death, 1 Chronicles
s: caused_by Saul's trespass Saul dies by falling on his own sword after his armor bearer, terrified, refuses to thrust him through. The armor bearer then also falls on his sword and dies, and Saul dies with his three sons and all his house together. The Philistines mutilate and display his body parts, while Jabesh Gilead later buries his bones.

l: Saul's trespass, 1 Chronicles
s: Saul's trespass against the LORD: disobedience, not keeping the LORD's word, and consulting a familiar spirit instead of inquiring of the LORD. Chapter 10 states it led to his death.

l: Jebusites, 1 Chronicles
s: inhabit Jerusalem [inhabitants of the land, then called Jebus] The Jebusites are the inhabitants of the land at Jebus. They tell David he will not come in, but David nevertheless takes the stronghold of Zion.

l: mighty men of David, 1 Chronicles
s: The mighty men are listed as those who showed themselves strong with David in his kingdom and with all Israel to make him king. The chapter names Jashobeam, chief of the thirty, Eleazar, Abishai, Benaiah, and a long roster of others, including Uriah the Hittite, with their origins and some of their deeds.

l: the three, 1 Chronicles
s: The three mighty men break through the Philistine army to draw water from the well of Bethlehem and bring it to David, who will not drink it. Abishai is chief of the three but not included among them, and Benaiah gains a name among them but does not attain to them. Jashobeam and Eleazar are also named as among the leading mighty men.

l: well of Bethlehem, 1 Chronicles
s: The well of Bethlehem, by the gate, is what David longs to drink from. Three mighty men break through the Philistine army to draw its water, but David pours it out to the LORD instead of drinking it.

l: Sibbecai the Hushathite, 1 Chronicles
s: Sibbecai the Hushathite, a Zerahite, commands the eighth monthly division and kills the giant's son Sippai at Gezer, helping subdue the Philistine giants.

l: covenant at Hebron, 1 Chronicles
s: David makes a covenant with all the elders of Israel at Hebron before the LORD. After it, they anoint him king over Israel according to the LORD's word by Samuel.

l: capture of Jebus, 1 Chronicles
s: has_result David's city [David took the stronghold of Zion] David and all Israel go to Jebus, where the inhabitants tell him he will not come in, yet he takes the stronghold of Zion, which becomes David's city. Joab goes up first and is made chief, as David had promised. David then lives in the stronghold and builds the city around it.

l: army (David's army), 1 Chronicles
s: is_a great army like God's army [grew as men came daily to David] David's army grew day by day as men came to help him until it was a great army like God's army. Its tribal contingents at Hebron are numbered, including Simeon seven thousand one hundred, Levi four thousand six hundred, Ephraim twenty thousand eight hundred, Zebulun fifty thousand, Naphtali thirty-seven thousand with a thousand captains, Dan twenty-eight thousand six hundred, Asher forty thousand, and one hundred twenty thousand from east of the Jordan.

l: feast at Hebron (David's coronation), 1 Chronicles
s: After the tribes made David king at Hebron, they stayed three days eating and drinking on provisions their brothers supplied. Neighbors from Issachar, Zebulun and Naphtali brought abundant food by animal, and joy filled Israel.

l: Obed-Edom, 1 Chronicles
s: Obed-Edom is a Gittite whose house the LORD blessed after he received the ark of God for three months, when David would not move it to David's city. Later he appears as a doorkeeper, son of Jeduthun and Hosah, blessed by God with eight sons and grandsons through Shemaiah. With sons and relatives, sixty-two able men served; the lot gave him the south gate and his sons the storehouse.

l: Baal Perazim, 1 Chronicles
s: Baal Perazim is the place of David's first battle, where he and his men defeat the Philistines; it is named after David's declaration that God broke his enemies by his hand like waters breaking out.

l: building materials (David's preparations), 1 Chronicles
s: David's preparations of building materials for the LORD's house: abundant iron for nails and couplings, bronze without weight, countless cedar from Sidonians and Tyre, vast gold and silver, plus timber, stone and many skilled workmen. The records list the materials, then end with Solomon being told he may add to them.

l: Michal, 1 Chronicles
s: Michal, Saul's daughter, watches from a window as the ark enters David's city, sees king David dancing and playing, and despises him in her heart.

l: procession bringing the ark up to Jerusalem, 1 Chronicles
s: includes David [with elders and captains, joyfully] The procession carried the ark up from the house of Obed-Edom to David's city with David, the elders, and the captains over thousands, after the Levites had sanctified themselves. Seven bulls and seven rams were sacrificed, priests blew trumpets, and all Israel sounded cornets, trumpets, cymbals, stringed instruments, and harps with shouting. It ended with the ark's arrival in David's city, where Michal watched from a window.

l: Hosah, 1 Chronicles
s: Hosah, a descendant of Merari, had four named sons: Shimri, appointed chief by his father though not firstborn, then Hilkiah, Tebaliah, and Zechariah. Sons and brothers totaled thirteen. With Shuppim he received the western lot by the gate of Shallecheth at the ascending causeway.

l: offerings, 1 Chronicles
s: David offers burnt offerings and peace offerings before God when the ark is placed in the tent. Zadok and the priests are also assigned to offer burnt offerings continually, morning and evening, on the altar at the tabernacle in Gibeon according to the LORD's law.

l: thanksgiving song, 1 Chronicles
s: is_ordained_by David [first ordained that day, through Asaph and his brothers] On that day David first ordains giving thanks to the LORD through Asaph and his brothers, and the song is recorded in this chapter. It urges calling on the LORD, remembering his wonders and covenant, declaring his glory among the nations, and recognizing that the LORD made the heavens while other gods are idols. It ends with a petition for deliverance, a blessing of the LORD, and the people's "Amen."

l: David's house (dynasty), 1 Chronicles
s: David's house is the dynasty the LORD promises to build; David, amazed, prays for it to be established and blessed forever before the LORD, so the LORD's name may be magnified.

l: Davidic covenant promise, 1 Chronicles
s: is_a promise of an enduring house and kingdom [given by the LORD through Nathan] The LORD, through Nathan, promises David a house, an offspring to succeed him, and a throne and kingdom established forever, along with an enduring fatherly relationship. David accepts the promise in prayer, saying it gave him courage to pray, and asks that it be established forever as spoken, noting that the LORD has blessed the house and it is blessed forever.

l: Hadadezer, 1 Chronicles
s: Hadadezer, king of Zobah, owned cities Tibhath and Cun and warred with Tou of Hamath. David defeated him, destroying his chariots, horsemen and footmen, and seized gold shields and bronze; Tou then sent David greetings.

l: Syrians of Damascus, 1 Chronicles
s: serves David [became servants and brought tribute] The Syrians of Damascus come to help Hadadezer, and David strikes twenty-two thousand of their men. David then puts garrisons in Syria of Damascus, and the Syrians become his servants and bring tribute.

l: children of Ammon, 1 Chronicles
s: The Ammonite princes convinced Hanun that David's comforters were spies, leading to the humiliation of David's servants. Seeing they had become odious to David, the Ammonites hired foreign forces and gathered from their cities for battle at the city gate. They fled before Abishai when the Syrians fled, retreating into their city, and were left without Syrian help after Hadadezer's servants made peace with David. The children of Ammon had their country wasted by Joab's army, and their cities were treated as Rabbah's people were. Their king's crown was taken by David, and the people of their cities were cut with saws, iron picks, and axes.

l: Hanun, 1 Chronicles
s: Hanun, son of Nahash, succeeds him as Ammonite king. Heeding suspicious princes, he humiliates David's comforting messengers by shaving them and cutting their garments, then hires chariots and horsemen with a thousand talents of silver.

l: David's servants, 1 Chronicles
s: David's servants went to Hanun in the land of the Ammonites to comfort him over his father's death. They were shaved and had their garments cut off at the buttocks, then sent away greatly humiliated. David told them to stay at Jericho until their beards had grown, and then return.

l: Syrians, 1 Chronicles
s: has_disposition will not help the children of Ammon [after defeat by Israel] The Syrians fled before Joab and later called out more Syrians from beyond the River under Shophach, captain of Hadadezer's army. David defeated them, killing seven thousand charioteers, forty thousand footmen, and Shophach. Hadadezer's servants then made peace with David, served him, and would no longer help the Ammonites.

l: mercenary force (hired by Ammon), 1 Chronicles
s: A mercenary force of thirty-two thousand chariots and the king of Maacah with his people, hired by the Ammonites for a thousand talents of silver, camped near Medeba apart from them, and fled when Joab advanced.

l: war between Israel and Ammon/Syrians, 1 Chronicles
s: A war between Israel and Ammon with hired Syrians, caused by Hanun's humiliation of David's servants. Joab and Abishai routed the enemy at the gate; David defeated a second Syrian force under Shophach across the Jordan. Syrians made peace, abandoning Ammon; Israel won.

l: Rabbah, 1 Chronicles
s: Rabbah was besieged by Joab, struck, and overthrown. David took the king's crown, much plunder, and the people from the city.

l: Elhanan the son of Jair, 1 Chronicles
s: is_son_of Jair In another war with the Philistines, Elhanan the son of Jair killed Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite. Lahmi's spear had a staff like a weaver's beam.

l: man of great stature (at Gath), 1 Chronicles
s: A man of great stature at Gath, born to a giant, with six fingers and six toes on each hand and foot; he defied Israel during a war and was killed by Jonathan son of Shimea.

l: Jonathan the son of Shimea, 1 Chronicles
s: Jonathan, son of Shimea and brother of David, is identified by his family ties and ultimately kills the giant of Gath who defied Israel.

l: giant (of Gath), 1 Chronicles
s: A giant of Gath whose offspring, including Sippai, Lahmi and the six-fingered man, were born there and all ultimately killed by David and his servants.

l: war with the Philistines, 1 Chronicles
s: Three engagements are recorded: at Gezer, where Sibbecai killed Sippai; another where Elhanan killed Lahmi; and at Gath, where Jonathan killed a man of great stature. Each ended with a giant of the Philistines slain, and the first is said to have ended with the Philistines subdued.

l: Satan, 1 Chronicles
s: Satan stands up against Israel and moves David to take a census of Israel. He appears only at the start of the chapter, as the instigator of the census.

l: Ornan the Jebusite, 1 Chronicles
s: Ornan, a Jebusite with four sons, owns a threshing floor; he sees the angel while threshing, offers everything free to David, but David insists on paying, so Ornan sells it for six hundred gold shekels.

l: angel (the LORD's angel), 1 Chronicles
s: The LORD's angel is a destroying messenger sent to Jerusalem during the pestilence. Told to withdraw his hand, he stands at Ornan's threshing floor with drawn sword; David sees him, raises an altar and sacrifices, and the angel sheathes his sword.

l: census of Israel, 1 Chronicles
s: A census instigated by Satan and ordered by David, carried out by Joab, counting 1,100,000 swordsmen in Israel and 470,000 in Judah, omitting Levi and Benjamin; it displeased God, brought a strike on Israel, and David confessed sin.

l: pestilence, 1 Chronicles
s: A plague sent by the LORD on Israel, chosen by David as the third option of three days of the angel destroying; seventy thousand men die before the LORD relents and it stops.

l: threshing floor of Ornan, 1 Chronicles
s: purchase_price 600 shekels of gold [paid by David] The threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite is where the LORD's angel stands when the LORD relents from destroying Jerusalem. David buys it for six hundred shekels of gold as the site for an altar, so that the plague may be stopped.

l: altar (David's altar to the LORD), 1 Chronicles
s: An altar David builds on Ornan's threshing floor at the angel's command; he offers burnt and peace offerings, the LORD answers by fire from the sky, and David sacrifices there while the tabernacle remains at Gibeon.

l: three choices of punishment, 1 Chronicles
s: Three punishments the LORD offers David through Gad: three years of famine, three months of defeat by foes, or three days of pestilence from the LORD's sword. David chooses to fall into the LORD's hand, trusting his great mercies, rather than man's hand.

l: princes of Israel, 1 Chronicles
s: The princes of Israel are officials summoned by David to Jerusalem, where they hear him explain the LORD's choice of Solomon and are charged to keep the LORD's commandments and help Solomon.

l: Shelomoth, 1 Chronicles
s: Shelomoth, a descendant of Eliezer through Rehabiah, Jeshaiah, Joram and Zichri, oversaw with his brothers all the treasuries of dedicated things given by David, Samuel, Saul, Abner, Joab and others.

l: Levite census, 1 Chronicles
s: counts Levites [from twenty years old and upward, by David's last words] The Levites aged thirty and up were counted at thirty-eight thousand by their polls, man by man. A further count by David's last words registered the heads of fathers' houses from twenty years old and upward, in the number of names.

l: Levite divisions and duties, 1 Chronicles
s: David organized the Levites by Levi's sons Gershon, Kohath, and Merari, assigning 24,000 to oversee the work, 6,000 as officers and judges, 4,000 as doorkeepers, and 4,000 as musicians. Their duties covered Tent of Meeting service, purifying holy things, preparing offerings, daily morning and evening thanks and praise, and burnt offerings at set times.

l: Ahimelech, 1 Chronicles
s: Ahimelech, a descendant of Ithamar and son of Abiathar, helped David and Zadok divide the priests by service, present as lots were cast and recorded.

l: division of priestly service by lot, 1 Chronicles
s: An impartial drawing of twenty-four lots divided priestly service between Eleazar's and Ithamar's lines, both having sanctuary princes. Following Aaron's ordinance, the first lot fell to Jehoiarib, the second to Jedaiah, through Maaziah twenty-fourth; Shemaiah recorded it before the king, princes, Zadok, Ahimelech, and household heads.

l: musicians' service, 1 Chronicles
s: The musicians' service was prophesying with harps, stringed instruments, and cymbals in the LORD's house; David and the army captains set it apart, and it was organized under Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman, who answered to the king.

l: musicians (the instructed singers), 1 Chronicles
s: has_number 288 [including their brothers, all skillful] The singers, together with their brothers who were instructed in singing to the LORD and were skillful, numbered two hundred eighty-eight. They were all included in the casting of lots for their offices.

l: casting of lots, 1 Chronicles
s: determines offices of the musicians [all alike, small and great, teacher and student] The musicians cast lots for their offices, all alike, small and great, teacher and student. The lots determined the order of the twenty-four divisions, beginning with Joseph of Asaph's house.

l: twenty-four divisions, 1 Chronicles
s: Twenty-four divisions assigned by lot, each a leader with sons and brothers totaling twelve, running from the first lot, Joseph of Asaph, to the twenty-fourth, Romamti-Ezer.

l: doorkeepers, 1 Chronicles
s: The doorkeepers were Levite guards ministering in the LORD's house, drawn from Korahite divisions and the sons of Merari. Gates were assigned by lot, by fathers' houses, small and great alike. Posts ranged from six on the east to four daily north and south, two at the storehouse, and six on the west.

l: lot casting, 1 Chronicles
s: Lot casting, by fathers' houses and small and great alike, assigned the gates: east to Shelemiah, north to his son Zechariah, south to Obed-Edom with the storehouse to his sons, west to Shuppim and Hosah.

l: treasuries, 1 Chronicles
s: ruled_by Shebuel [son of Gershom, son of Moses] Ahijah was over the treasures of God's house, and Zetham and Joel, sons of Jehieli the Gershonite, were over the treasures of the LORD's house. Shebuel son of Gershom, son of Moses, was ruler over the treasuries.

l: dedicated things, 1 Chronicles
s: Dedicated things are gifts consecrated by King David, household heads, captains, and earlier figures like Samuel, Saul, Abner and Joab, partly from battle plunder, meant for repairing the LORD's house and kept by Shelomoth and his brothers.

l: Jerijah, 1 Chronicles
s: Jerijah was chief of the Hebronites by generations and fathers' households. In David's fortieth year they were sought out, and mighty men of valor were found at Jazer of Gilead; 2,700 relatives became overseers of Reubenites.

l: census, 1 Chronicles
s: Joab began a census in Israel but left it unfinished; it brought wrath on Israel, and the number was never entered in King David's chronicles. Those twenty and under were uncounted, given the LORD's promise of stars-like increase.

l: twelve monthly divisions, 1 Chronicles
s: Twelve rotating divisions of 24,000 men each serve David month by month through the year, each under a named captain, from Jashobeam in the first month, through Benaiah and Asahel, to Heldai in the twelfth.

l: tribal rulers (tribes of Israel), 1 Chronicles
s: is_a captains of the tribes of Israel Each tribe of Israel had a named ruler, including Eliezer over the Reubenites, Zadok for Aaron, Elihu of Judah, and Azarel of Dan. Half-tribes of Manasseh had two rulers, Joel and Iddo, and the passage calls them the captains of the tribes of Israel.

l: royal property managers (David's property), 1 Chronicles
s: manages David [property belonging to David] Named officials oversaw King David's property: Azmaveth and Jonathan over the treasures, Ezri over field work, Shimei and Zabdi over vineyards and wine, Baal Hanan and Joash over olive and sycamore trees and oil, and others over herds, camels, donkeys, and flocks. The text calls them all rulers of the property which was King David's.

l: temple plans, 1 Chronicles
s: Plans for the temple, the LORD's house, which David gives to Solomon. They cover the porch, rooms, treasuries, courts, priestly and Levite divisions, and vessels, with gold and silver specified by weight. David says the pattern came in writing from the LORD's hand, partly by the Spirit.

l: leaders who offered willingly, 1 Chronicles
s: gave_to house of God (temple) [willingly, for its service] The princes of the fathers' households, the princes of the tribes, the captains of thousands and hundreds, and the rulers over the king's work respond to David's call by offering willingly. Their gifts are five thousand talents and ten thousand darics of gold, ten thousand talents of silver, eighteen thousand talents of bronze, and one hundred thousand talents of iron. Their willing, wholehearted giving causes the people and David to rejoice.

l: offerings for the temple, 1 Chronicles
s: Temple offerings begin with David's gifts of Ophir gold and refined silver from his own treasure; leaders add gold, silver, bronze, iron, and others give precious stones, stored under Jehiel the Gershonite. David concludes everything came from the LORD.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles
s: The Second Book of Chronicles narrates the reigns of Solomon and the kings of Judah, from the height of the united kingdom to the destruction of Jerusalem and a hopeful close. The central theme is that kings prosper when they seek the LORD and suffer when they forsake him, with the temple at the center of the story. Chapters 1-9 cover Solomon. God grants him wisdom at Gibeon, and he gathers great wealth. With Huram of Tyre supplying timber and the craftsman Huram-abi, Solomon builds the temple on Mount Moriah, makes its furnishings, and brings in the ark. God's glory fills the house. Solomon prays at the dedication, fire falls from heaven, and the LORD warns that forsaking him will bring uprooting. The queen of Sheba visits, and Solomon dies after forty years, succeeded by Rehoboam. Chapters 10-12 describe the split of the kingdom. Rehoboam rejects the elders' counsel and answers the people harshly, so Israel departs under Jeroboam. Rehoboam abandons the law, and Shishak of Egypt plunders Jerusalem. Abijah (ch. 13) defeats Jeroboam's larger army by relying on God. Chapters 14-20 cover Asa and Jehoshaphat. Asa removes idols, defeats Zerah's million-strong force, and renews the covenant, but late in life relies on Syria, imprisons the seer Hanani, and seeks only physicians in his illness. Jehoshaphat teaches the law and appoints judges. He allies with Ahab, who dies in battle despite Micaiah's warning, and Jehoshaphat is rebuked by Jehu. When Moab and Ammon attack, Judah is saved by praise and trust. Chapters 21-28 trace decline. Jehoram, Ahaziah, and Athaliah follow Ahab's house, and Athaliah destroys the royal offspring until Jehoiada hides and later crowns Joash. Joash repairs the temple but turns to idols after Jehoiada dies and has Zechariah stoned. Amaziah worships Edomite gods and is defeated by Israel. Uzziah prospers but is struck with leprosy for burning incense. Jotham does right. Ahaz is the worst, sacrificing children and closing the LORD's house. Chapters 29-35 describe revival. Hezekiah cleanses the temple, keeps a great Passover, and reorganizes the priests' support. He and Isaiah pray, and an angel destroys Sennacherib's army. Manasseh sins grievously, is taken to Babylon in chains, repents, and is restored. Amon is killed. Josiah purges the land, finds the book of the law, and keeps a great Passover, but dies fighting Neco at Megiddo. Chapter 36 recounts the last kings, Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, and Zedekiah. The people mock the prophets, Nebuchadnezzar's Chaldeans burn the temple and Jerusalem, and survivors are exiled to Babylon for seventy years. The book ends with Cyrus of Persia proclaiming that the LORD's house is to be built in Jerusalem and that God's people may go up.

l: Solomon, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Solomon is the son of David and his successor as king of Israel, firmly established in his kingdom with the LORD with him and delighting in him. Early on he offers a thousand burnt offerings at Gibeon and asks God for wisdom and knowledge; God grants it and promises riches, wealth and honor unmatched by any king before or after him. He gathers chariots, horsemen and horses from Egypt and Kue, and reigns from Jerusalem. What matters most about him is his building of the LORD's house. He decides to build a house for the LORD's name and one for his kingdom, enlisting tens of thousands of laborers and asking Huram of Tyre for a craftsman and Lebanon timber. He begins the temple on Mount Moriah in the fourth year of his reign, overlaying it with gold and making the cherubim, veil and the pillars Jachin and Boaz. He makes the bronze altar, basins, lamp stands, tables, courts and golden vessels, casting bronze in the Jordan plain. He then brings the ark up, prays at length, offers vast sacrifices, and holds a seven-day feast. The LORD appears to him, promising to establish his throne if he walks as David did and warning of consequences if he turns away. Over twenty years he completes the LORD's house and his own, rebuilds cities, prevails against Hamath Zobah, builds Tadmor, and conscripts forced labor from other peoples but not Israelites. He moves Pharaoh's daughter to her own house, organizes priests, Levites and doorkeepers per David's ordinance, and receives gold from Ophir through ships sent by Huram. His fame brings the queen of Sheba, whose questions he answers, and tribute from kings of the earth and Arabia. He owns an ivory throne overlaid with gold, hundreds of gold shields, and ships of Tarshish, and rules from the River to the Philistines' land and Egypt's border. He reigns forty years in Jerusalem, dies, is buried in David's city, and is succeeded by his son Rehoboam. The final chapter recalls Rehoboam making the people's yoke heavy, with Jeroboam having fled Solomon's presence to Egypt.

l: David, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: David is a king of Israel and man of God, father of Solomon. He wished to build a house for the LORD's name, and the LORD said he did well but forbade it, assigning the task to his son. Chosen over Israel and promised a throne, he dedicated treasures and kept weapons in God's house. Solomon asks the LORD to remember David's kindnesses.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: The LORD is the God of Israel, of the fathers, of David, Solomon, Judah and its kings. He is creator of heaven and earth, greater than all gods, dwelling in heaven and thick darkness, yet not contained by heaven itself. He alone knows human hearts. He is described as good, righteous, gracious, merciful and compassionate, with enduring loving kindness. He has no iniquity, no partiality and takes no bribes. He made a covenant with Israel at Horeb after the exodus from Egypt, chose Jerusalem for his name, chose David, and gave David's line the kingdom by a covenant of salt and the promise of a lamp. The records are chiefly about his dealings with Judah's kings from Solomon to the exile. In the early chapters he makes Solomon exceedingly great, grants him wisdom and riches, fills the house with glory and fire, and promises to hear, forgive and heal if his people humble themselves, while warning of uprooting if they serve other gods. Under Rehoboam he forbids war with the northern brothers and, after the people humble themselves, spares them from destruction. He strikes Jeroboam and Israel before Abijah. He gives rest to Asa, strikes the Ethiopians, and is found by those who seek him. He is with Jehoshaphat, establishes his kingdom, fights for Judah in battle, and also sends a lying spirit against Ahab and judges alliances with the wicked. Where kings forsake him he judges them: Jehoram is struck with disease, Joash and Amaziah suffer defeat, Uzziah is struck with leprosy, and Ahaz brings Judah low. He is not with Israel. Where they humble themselves he relents, as with Hezekiah, for whom he saves Jerusalem from Sennacherib by an angel, and with Manasseh. Through Huldah he declares curses on Jerusalem but promises Josiah a peaceful death. At the end he sends messengers out of compassion, then brings the Chaldeans when there is no remedy, fulfilling Jeremiah's seventy years of desolation. He then stirs Cyrus to proclaim the rebuilding of his house. Overall the pattern is that seeking him brings blessing and rest, and forsaking him brings wrath, yet his covenant and compassion persist.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Israel is both a people and the land or kingdom they occupy, as presented in 2 Chronicles. It is the people the LORD brought out of Egypt, in covenant with him (the covenant stored in the ark), and given a land said to stretch from Hamath or Dan in the north to the brook of Egypt or Beersheba in the south. Solomon calls it a great people, countless as the dust. Early on, the whole assembly gathers at Jerusalem, sacrifices in vast numbers before the ark, and watches fire come down at the temple dedication. Solomon prays that the LORD would hear and forgive them after defeat, drought, famine, plague or captivity, and return them to their land if they repent. The LORD warns that if they forsake him he will pluck them from the land he gave. The pivotal break comes at Shechem: when Rehoboam refuses to lighten the yoke, Israel declares no portion in David, stones Hadoram, and rebels against David's house, a rebellion that continues to this day. Rehoboam is forbidden to fight them, since the LORD calls them brothers of Judah, and faithful priests, Levites and others leave for Judah. Under Jeroboam the northern kingdom keeps golden calves worshipped as gods and a priesthood of its own making, not of Aaron's line, and drives out the LORD's priests. Abijah's Judah defeats it, with 500,000 chosen men falling. Later records show a mixed relationship: hired Israelite troops are sent home and raid Judah's cities; Joash of Israel defeats Judah, breaks Jerusalem's wall and takes plunder and hostages to Samaria; Israel strikes Ahaz and takes 200,000 captives, but after Oded's rebuke its armed men release them. Many people come over to Asa when they see the LORD with him, though the high places remain. Hezekiah's invitation from Beersheba to Dan to keep the Passover is mocked by many in Ephraim and Manasseh, yet some from Asher, Manasseh and Zebulun humble themselves and come. The account ends with Israelites present destroying pillars, Asherah poles, high places and altars across Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim and Manasseh, then giving tithes and first fruits abundantly, a partial return to the LORD.

l: Gibeon, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: has high place Gibeon is the site of the high place where Solomon and the assembly go, because God's Tent of Meeting is there. Solomon offers a thousand burnt offerings there, and God appears to him that night; he then leaves Gibeon for Jerusalem.

l: Tent of Meeting, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: A sacred tent made by Moses in the wilderness, now located at the high place at Gibeon, where Solomon and the assembly go and the bronze altar stands before it.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Jerusalem is the city the LORD chose out of all the tribes of Israel to put his name there forever, and it houses the LORD's house and the king's house. It first appears as the place where David pitched a tent for God's ark. Under Solomon it flourishes: he returns there from Gibeon, keeps chariots and horsemen there, reigns forty years over all Israel, receives the queen of Sheba, and makes silver, gold, and cedars as common as stones and sycamores. His son Rehoboam then lives and reigns there seventeen years, and Levites and those from all the tribes who seek the LORD come to sacrifice. After this height, the city's history is marked by threat, decline, and renewal. Shishak attacks, and though devastation is averted when the king and princes humble themselves, he takes the treasures. Jehoshaphat appoints Levites, priests, and family heads to give judgment there. Under Joash, idolatry after Jehoiada's death brings wrath and Syrian attack; later Joash of Israel breaks down four hundred cubits of the wall and takes treasures, and a conspiracy forms against Amaziah. Hezekiah's reign brings a great Passover assembly with altars thrown into the Kidron and joy unmatched since Solomon, and the LORD saves the city from Sennacherib, whose men shouted at the people on the wall. Manasseh, returned from Babylon, builds a high outer wall and casts out foreign altars. Josiah purges idolatry, and the inhabitants gather at the LORD's house to join the covenant. The account ends with Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, and Zedekiah reigning in turn, the wall broken down and palaces burned by the Chaldeans, and finally Cyrus commanding that a house for the LORD be built there.

l: bronze altar, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: A bronze altar made by Bezalel, son of Uri, son of Hur, stands before the LORD's tabernacle at Gibeon, where Solomon goes up and offers one thousand burnt offerings.

l: Solomon's request for wisdom, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: is_a request for wisdom and knowledge [to judge God's people]

l: Huram, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Huram is the king of Tyre who blesses the LORD, God of Israel, and serves Solomon. In Chapter 2 he replies in writing, agrees to send Lebanon wood by sea in rafts to Joppa, asks for promised wheat, barley, oil and wine, and sends the skilled Huram-abi. In Chapter 4, Huram, also called Huram-abi, makes the bronze work for God's house: two pillars with capitals, bowls, networks and four hundred pomegranates, bases with basins, pots, shovels, forks, and the sea with twelve oxen. He also gives cities to Solomon and sends ships and servants.

l: Huram-abi, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Huram-abi is a skillful, understanding man of mixed descent: his mother was from the daughters of Dan, his father a Tyrian. Huram sends him to Solomon. Master of metalwork, stone, timber, textiles and engraving, he is to work alongside Solomon's skillful men and those of David.

l: LORD's temple, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: The LORD's temple is the house Solomon built in Jerusalem for the name of the LORD, on Mount Moriah at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, where the LORD had appeared to David. Solomon planned it as a great and wonderful house, greater because God is greater than all gods, and gathered workers, craftsmen, timber, and provisions. Its purposes were burning incense, the continual show bread, and burnt offerings on mornings, evenings, Sabbaths, new moons, and set feasts. Its foundation measured sixty by twenty cubits, with a porch across the front. Beams, thresholds, walls, and doors were overlaid with gold and engraved with cherubim, and the larger room had a cypress ceiling overlaid with fine gold, ornamented with palm trees and chains. Precious stones and gold from Parvaim adorned it. A veil of blue, purple, crimson, and fine linen, ornamented with cherubim, marked the most holy place. Furnishings included ten gold lamp stands, ten tables, the sea, basins, and the golden altar; the inner doors were gold, and the courts had bronze-overlaid doors. Treasuries held the dedicated silver, gold, and vessels. When the work was completed from foundation to finish, the ark was installed in the inner sanctuary and a cloud of the LORD's glory filled the house so that the priests could not enter. The king and people dedicated it. Solomon admitted that even heaven cannot contain God, yet asked that God's eyes be open toward it and that prayers of Israelites and foreigners directed there be heard. The LORD said he had chosen and made it holy so his name would be there forever, but warned that if the people turned away he would cast it out of his sight and make it a byword. The later records show that decline. Uzziah entered to burn incense and was struck with leprosy and cut off from the house. Manasseh set altars and an idol in its courts, then after his restoration removed them. Josiah repaired it with money gathered by the Levites, and the book of the law was found there. Finally, under Nebuchadnezzar, its vessels were carried off to Babylon in stages, the people polluted it, and the Chaldeans killed young men in the sanctuary, took its treasures, and burned it. The records end with Cyrus commanded to build a house for the LORD in Jerusalem.

l: Judah, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Judah is a kingdom and people, centered on Jerusalem, whose fortunes rise and fall with the faithfulness of its kings. It holds a covenant with the LORD, has priests (sons of Aaron) and Levites, and maintains Temple worship with daily offerings, incense, show bread and the lamp stand. The records follow it through successive reigns. Under Rehoboam it is fortified and strengthened by Levites, priests and faithful Israelites. Under Abijah it defeats Israel's larger army by crying to the LORD. Under Asa it seeks the LORD, builds fortified cities, enjoys quiet, defeats the Ethiopians, swears an oath with all its heart, and has rest for many years. Under Jehoshaphat it brings tribute, is garrisoned, taught from the law, and given judges; high places are removed, though hearts are not fully set on God. It is delivered without fighting when it gathers to seek the LORD, and it returns to Jerusalem rejoicing. Decline follows. Jehoram leads it astray with high places; Edom and Libnah revolt, and Philistines and Arabians plunder the king's house. After Jehoiada's death its princes turn to Asherah poles and idols, and Syrians destroy its princes. Under Amaziah it supplies 300,000 men but is defeated by Israel at Beth Shemesh and raided by dismissed Israelite soldiers. Under Ahaz it suffers heavy losses, including 120,000 men in a day, captivity, and raids by Edomites and Philistines, while Ahaz builds high places for other gods in every city. Renewal comes under Hezekiah: God gives one heart to obey the king and princes, the assembly rejoices, idols are broken down, and tithes and dedicated things are brought. Sennacherib's invasion is survived through the LORD, and wrath over Hezekiah's pride is averted when he humbles himself. Manasseh seduces Judah into greater evil, but after his repentance it serves the LORD, though it still sacrifices at high places. After Amon's death the people of the land make Josiah king. Josiah purges high places, Asherah poles and images, the people hear the book of the covenant, curses are declared against the place, and throughout his days Judah does not depart from following the LORD.

l: burden bearers (Solomon's), The Second Book of Chronicles
s: has_count seventy thousand Solomon counts out seventy thousand men to bear burdens for the building work. The same number of the foreigners in Israel are later set to bear burdens as well.

l: stone cutters (Solomon's), The Second Book of Chronicles
s: has_count eighty thousand [in the mountains] Solomon counts out eighty thousand men as stone cutters in the mountains, with overseers set over them. Eighty thousand of the foreigners are later also set as stone cutters in the mountains.

l: foreigners in Israel, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Foreigners residing in Israel, counted by Solomon after David's census at 153,600, are assigned to labor: 70,000 burden bearers, 80,000 stone cutters in the mountains, and 3,600 overseers directing the people's work.

l: timber (cedar, cypress, algum), The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Timber of cedar, cypress, and algum grows in Lebanon and is used for terraces of the LORD's and king's houses and for harps. Solomon requests it from Huram, offering food and drink; Huram agrees to cut it and raft it to Joppa for carrying to Jerusalem.

l: temple (the LORD's house), The Second Book of Chronicles
s: The temple, the LORD's house, appears first as Solomon's work: its most holy place measured twenty cubits by twenty, overlaid with six hundred talents of fine gold, with fifty-shekel gold nails and two carved cherubim inside. Later it is neglected under Ahaz, doors shut, lamps out, vessels discarded. Hezekiah reopens, repairs, and cleanses it, restoring worship, sacrifice, song, and ordered service.

l: cherubim (in the most holy place), The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Two carved cherubim, overlaid with gold, stand in the most holy place. Each has five-cubit wings, reaching the wall and touching each other, spanning twenty cubits together. They stand on their feet facing the house, wings spread over the ark's place.

l: Jachin, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: is_a pillar [on the right hand] Jachin is the name Solomon gave to the pillar set up on the right hand before the temple.

l: Boaz, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: is_a pillar [on the left hand] Boaz is the name Solomon gave to the pillar set up on the left hand before the temple.

l: pillars (before the temple), The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Two pillars made by Solomon stand before the LORD's house, thirty-five cubits high with five-cubit capitals. Chains and one hundred pomegranates adorn their tops. Set one on the right and one on the left, they are named Jachin and Boaz.

l: building of the temple, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: begins_on second day of the second month [fourth year of Solomon's reign] The building began on the second day of the second month in the fourth year of Solomon's reign, on the site David had prepared and appointed. The foundations were laid by the first measure of sixty by twenty cubits, and the work included extensive gold overlay, precious stones, carved cherubim, a veil, and two front pillars.

l: molten sea, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: The molten sea is a large round basin, ten cubits across brim to brim, five cubits high, thirty cubits around, a handbreadth thick, with a cup- or lily-shaped brim. It holds three thousand baths and serves the priests for washing. It rests on twelve oxen facing the four directions, three each, and is placed on the right side of God's house, eastward toward the south.

l: ark of the LORD's covenant, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: The ark of the LORD's covenant, originally in Zion, David's city, was brought up by Levites and Levitical priests with the Tent of Meeting and its holy vessels. Priests placed it in the most holy place beneath the cherubim's wings. Its long poles' ends show toward the inner sanctuary only, and it holds just Moses's two tablets from Horeb.

l: Levites, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: The Levites are a chosen group, set apart by the LORD to stand before him, minister and burn incense. Across the records they serve as ark-bearers, singers and musicians with David's instruments, teachers of all Israel who are holy to the LORD, guards of the king, officers before the judges, and helpers in sacrifice. Early on they take up the ark and the singers stand at the altar's east end. Later, named Levites (Shemaiah, Nethaniah, Zebadiah, Asahel, Shemiramoth, Jehonathan, Adonijah, Tobijah, Tobadonijah) are sent with princes and priests to teach the book of the LORD's law in Judah's cities. Under Jehoiada they are gathered to Jerusalem as gatekeepers in three groups, surrounding the king with weapons and keeping both Sabbath shifts on duty. Under Hezekiah they sanctify themselves and carry uncleanness out of the house to the brook Kidron, play instruments and sing, and help skin burnt offerings, being more upright in heart than the priests in sanctifying themselves. Some Levites were ashamed, then sanctified themselves, and killed Passovers for those not clean, handing blood to the priests. Under Josiah they return the ark to Solomon's house, prepare by divisions, kill and roast the Passover, and provide offerings for themselves, the priests, singers and gatekeepers, while their chiefs donate five thousand small livestock and five hundred cattle. Their role thus runs from carrying and teaching to guarding and sacrificial service.

l: priests, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Levitical priests, all sanctified and not keeping their divisions, bring the ark into the most holy place under the cherubim's wings; 120 sound trumpets, then a cloud prevents them from standing to minister.

l: Levite singers, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Levite singers led by Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun, with their sons and brothers, stand at the altar's east end in fine linen with cymbals, stringed instruments and harps, joining trumpeters in one sound praising the LORD.

l: cloud (filling the LORD's house), The Second Book of Chronicles
s: fills house of the LORD (Solomon's temple) [after the praise] A cloud filled the LORD's house as the singers and trumpeters praised him. It prevented the priests from standing to minister, because it signified that the LORD's glory filled God's house.

l: praise of the LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: has_content he is good, his loving kindness endures forever [words sung by trumpeters and singers] The trumpeters and singers were as one, lifting their voices with trumpets, cymbals, and instruments to praise and thank the LORD, saying he is good and his loving kindness endures forever. The house was then filled with a cloud.

l: covenant with David, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Solomon says the LORD has fulfilled his promise to David by putting Solomon on the throne of Israel and letting him build the house. He asks the LORD to keep the further promise that David will never lack a man to sit on the throne, on the condition that his children take heed to walk in the LORD's law. He asks that the LORD's word to David be verified.

l: Solomon's prayer of dedication, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Solomon's dedication prayer praises the LORD as incomparable and covenant-keeping, admits heaven cannot contain him and no man is sinless, and asks him to hear prayers toward the house, including foreigners and captives, in oaths, defeat, drought, famine, plague, battle and exile, ending by pleading for his resting place.

l: fire from heaven, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: consumed sacrifices and offerings [after Solomon's prayer] Fire comes down from heaven after Solomon finishes praying and consumes the burnt offering and the sacrifices. The people watching it bow to the ground, worship, and give thanks to the LORD.

l: sacrifices and offerings, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: The fire consumes the burnt offering and sacrifices, and the king and all the people offer sacrifices before the LORD, including Solomon's twenty-two thousand cattle and a hundred twenty thousand sheep. Because the bronze altar cannot receive the burnt offering, meal offering, and fat, Solomon makes the middle of the court holy to offer them there.

l: dedication feast, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Solomon and all Israel hold a seven-day dedication of the altar and a seven-day feast in the seventh month. Priests sound trumpets and Levites play David's instruments in thanks. A solemn assembly follows on the eighth day; on the twenty-third day the people go home joyful.

l: warning of judgment, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: A conditional warning from the LORD to Solomon: if he and the people turn away, forsake the statutes and serve other gods, they will be uprooted from the land and the house cast out, becoming a proverb and byword, with passersby told they abandoned the LORD.

l: cities built by Solomon, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Solomon built the cities Huram had given him and settled Israelites there, and built Tadmor, storage cities in Hamath, Beth Horon the upper and lower (fortified with walls, gates, and bars), and Baalath. He also built cities for his chariots and horsemen and whatever he desired in Jerusalem, Lebanon, and all his dominion.

l: remaining peoples conscripted for forced labor, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Surviving Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, left unconsumed by Israel, were conscripted by Solomon into forced labor that persisted to the writing's day, unlike Israelites, who served as warriors and officers.

l: burnt offerings, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Solomon offered burnt offerings to the LORD on the LORD's altar before the porch, as each day's duty required. He offered them according to Moses' commandment on the Sabbaths, new moons, and the three yearly feasts of unleavened bread, weeks, and booths.

l: feast of unleavened bread, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: duration seven days [then extended another seven days] A very great assembly kept the feast of unleavened bread in Jerusalem in the second month for seven days with great gladness, with the Levites and priests praising the LORD daily. The assembly then took counsel and kept another seven days with gladness.

l: priests, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Solomon appointed the divisions of the priests to their service according to the ordinance of David, who was called the man of God. The priests and Levites did not depart from the king's commandment concerning any matter or the treasures.

l: Levites, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Solomon appointed the Levites to their offices according to David's ordinance, to praise and minister before the priests as each day required. The doorkeepers served by divisions at every gate, and the Levites did not depart from the king's commandment concerning any matter or the treasures.

l: Edom, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Edom is a territory that revolted from Judah's rule in Jehoram's days and appointed its own king; Jehoram attacked the surrounding Edomites by night, yet Edom stays in revolt to this day.

l: queen of Sheba, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: The queen of Sheba, a ruler, travels with a great caravan to Jerusalem to test Solomon with hard questions. Overwhelmed by his wisdom and court, she affirms the report was true, blesses the LORD, gives him gold, spices and precious stones, then returns to her land.

l: Philistines, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: The Philistines are a people who first bring Jehoshaphat tribute of presents and silver, then, stirred up by the LORD against Jehoram, join Arabians to raid Judah, taking the king's possessions, sons and wives.

l: Jeroboam, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Jeroboam, son of Nebat and former servant of Solomon, rebelled against his lord and fled to Egypt. He returned when Israel sent for him, and with all Israel asked Rehoboam for a lighter yoke, fulfilling God's word spoken through Ahijah the Shilonite. As king of Israel, he cast off the Levites and priests, appointed his own priests for the high places, and made goat and golden calf idols as gods. He later set 800,000 chosen men against Abijah, but God struck Israel, costing him 500,000 men and several cities. He never regained strength, and the LORD struck him dead.

l: Rehoboam, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Rehoboam, son of Solomon and Naamah, was a king of Judah who lived in Jerusalem. At Shechem he rejected the old men's counsel and answered the people roughly, so he reigned only over the Israelites in Judah's cities; Judah and Benjamin were his. After Hadoram was stoned he fled to Jerusalem. Told by the LORD through Shemaiah not to fight Israel, he turned back from assembling 180,000 warriors and fortified cities for defense. He had eighteen wives, sixty concubines, twenty-eight sons and sixty daughters, loving Maacah most and appointing her son Abijah chief prince. Once strong, he abandoned the LORD's law with all Israel, then humbled himself after Shemaiah's message. Shishak took the gold shields, and he made bronze ones. He fought continual wars with Jeroboam. He began reigning at forty-one, ruled seventeen years, did evil by not seeking the LORD, was buried in David's city, and was succeeded by Abijah. His acts are recorded in the histories of Shemaiah and Iddo.

l: Solomon’s wisdom, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Solomon's wisdom is a God-given gift, put in his heart by the LORD. It enabled him to answer all the queen of Sheba's questions; she found its greatness exceeded its fame, and kings of the earth sought him, as he surpassed them in wisdom and riches.

l: Solomon’s riches, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Solomon's riches exceed all earth's kings. He receives 666 talents of gold yearly plus merchants', kings' and governors' tribute, makes gold shields, an ivory-and-gold throne and gold vessels, making silver valueless. Tarshish ships bring luxuries every three years; he keeps four thousand stalls and twelve thousand horsemen.

l: old men (Solomon's counselors), The Second Book of Chronicles
s: served Solomon [stood before him while he lived] The old men, who had stood before Solomon while he lived, are consulted by Rehoboam. They advise him to be kind, please the people and speak good words, so that the people will be his servants forever. Rehoboam abandons their counsel.

l: young men (Rehoboam's peers), The Second Book of Chronicles
s: grew_up_with Rehoboam [stood before him] The young men who grew up with Rehoboam and stood before him advise him to say that his little finger is thicker than his father's waist. They urge him to add to the yoke and chastise with scorpions rather than whips. Rehoboam follows their counsel.

l: David's house, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Israel renounces any portion or inheritance in David and the son of Jesse, telling David to see to his own house. Israel rebels against David's house, a state the text says continues to this day. Only the Israelites living in Judah's cities remain under Rehoboam.

l: heavy yoke (Solomon's burdens on Israel), The Second Book of Chronicles
s: was_imposed_by Solomon [described by Israel as grievous] The people describe the yoke and grievous service Solomon put on them and ask for it to be made lighter. Rehoboam instead promises to add to it, and sends Hadoram, who was over the men subject to forced labor. The yoke thus becomes the cause of Israel's break from Rehoboam.

l: Israel's rebellion (division of the kingdom), The Second Book of Chronicles
s: is_directed_against David's house [continuing to this day] After Rehoboam refuses to listen, Israel departs to their tents and only those in Judah's cities stay under him. The text says the outcome was brought about by God to establish his word through Ahijah. Israel's stoning of Hadoram and Rehoboam's flight to Jerusalem seal the break, which the text says lasts to this day.

l: fortified cities (Rehoboam's), The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Rehoboam's fortified cities are fifteen strongholds in Judah and Benjamin, including Bethlehem, Tekoa, Lachish and Hebron. He builds and fortifies them, stations captains with stores of food, oil and wine, equips each with shields and spears, and later disperses some of his sons among them.

l: Lachish, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Lachish is where Amaziah fled when the conspiracy against him arose in Jerusalem. His pursuers sent after him there and killed him.

l: priests and Levites, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Priests and Levites from all Israel abandon their pasture lands and possessions, relocating to Judah and Jerusalem to stand with Rehoboam, because Jeroboam and his sons cast them off from priestly service and appointed his own priests.

l: Maacah, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Maacah, Absalom's granddaughter, becomes Rehoboam's wife after Mahalath, bears Abijah, Attai, Ziza and Shelomith, and is loved above his other wives.

l: Abijah, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Abijah, a son of Rehoboam, is appointed chief and prince among his brothers because Rehoboam intends him to be king. He later reigns over Judah from Jerusalem for three years. Warring with Jeroboam, he relies on the LORD, and Judah prevails; he captures Bethel, Jeshanah, and Ephron with their villages. He grows mighty, takes fourteen wives, and fathers twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters. His remaining acts are recorded in the prophet Iddo's commentary, and he is buried in David's city.

l: Shishak, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Shishak is a king of Egypt who, in Rehoboam's fifth year, attacked Jerusalem with 1200 chariots, 60000 horsemen, and allied Lubim, Sukkiim, and Ethiopians. He seized Judah's fortified cities, then the temple and royal treasures plus Solomon's gold shields; Judah became servants, though Jerusalem escaped destruction by his hand.

l: Shemaiah, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: is_a prophet Shemaiah the prophet came to Rehoboam and the princes of Judah gathered at Jerusalem and told them the LORD had left them in Shishak's hand because they forsook him. He later received the LORD's word that they would be spared destruction. His histories are named as a record of Rehoboam's acts, along with those of Iddo the seer.

l: Ethiopians, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: The Ethiopians, Zerah's army, are struck by the LORD before Asa and Judah and flee. So many fall during the pursuit to Gerar that they cannot recover, and they are destroyed before the LORD and his army.

l: Shishak's invasion of Jerusalem, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: In Rehoboam's fifth year, Shishak invaded Judah with a huge army as punishment for trespassing against the LORD, seized fortified cities and reached Jerusalem; after leaders humbled themselves, Jerusalem survived, but treasures were plundered and Judah became servants.

l: Rehoboam's humbling, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: results_in turning of the LORD's wrath [not destroyed altogether] After Shemaiah's message, Rehoboam and the princes humbled themselves and said, "The LORD is righteous." Seeing this, the LORD promised some deliverance and no destruction, and his wrath turned from Rehoboam so that he was not destroyed altogether. The text also notes that good things were found in Judah.

l: battle between Abijah and Jeroboam, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: At Mount Zemaraim, Abijah's 400,000 men faced Jeroboam's 800,000, who ambushed Judah from behind. Judah cried to the LORD, trumpets sounded, and God struck Israel, killing 500,000. Judah won by relying on the LORD, then took Bethel, Jeshanah, Ephron.

l: Micaiah, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Micaiah, son of Imla and Uriel's child, is a prophet of the LORD whom Ahab hates for habitually prophesying evil. Urged to agree with other prophets, he swears to speak only God's word, mocks then truthfully warns of scattered Israel and a lying spirit, is struck by Zedekiah, imprisoned, and stakes his prophecy on Ahab's fate.

l: Asa, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Asa is a king of Judah, son of Abijah and Maacah's descendant line, who succeeds his father and begins by doing what is good and right in the LORD's eyes. He removes foreign altars, high places, pillars and Asherah poles, commands Judah to seek the LORD, and builds fortified cities during ten quiet years. He fields an army of 580,000 and, when Zerah attacks, cries to the LORD and pursues the fleeing Ethiopians to Gerar. Encouraged by prophecy, he renews the altar, leads a covenant gathering in his fifteenth year, and removes his mother Maacah as queen mother, though the high places remain. Later, facing Baasha, he pays Ben Hadad with temple and royal treasure instead of relying on the LORD. Rebuked by Hanani, he imprisons the seer and oppresses some people, and is told wars will follow. In his thirty-ninth year his feet are diseased; he seeks only physicians, dies in his forty-first year, and is buried in his own tomb in David's city.

l: Zerah the Ethiopian, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Zerah, an Ethiopian commander, marches against Asa with a million troops and three hundred chariots to Mareshah, but the LORD strikes his forces and they flee Asa and Judah.

l: Battle between Asa and Zerah, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Battle in the valley of Zephathah at Mareshah: after Asa's prayer, the LORD strikes the Ethiopians, who flee; Asa's army pursues them to Gerar and destroys them, then Judah plunders and returns to Jerusalem.

l: Azariah the son of Oded, The Second Book of Chronicles
